transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: Mon Jan 12 2026 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Video call
Attendees: Jenna (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ravi (CTO Helios), Sofia (ML Eng), Lena (Sec), Tomás (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): quick audit of current Helios prompt caching approach; main concerns about deterministic keying and accidental cross-tenant hits; plan to run bench and share security docs.

[00:00] Jenna (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. can we do quick intros? we'll try to keep this focused on cache keys, hit rates, and the safety surface area.
[00:18] Ravi (Helios): sure, ravi here. we run inference for robotics planning at the edge and in our cloud. Sofia is on the ML side, tomas on infra, lena handles security.
[00:30] Marcus (Redwood): quick note, our goal today is to walk through a proposed prefix signature scheme and identify any vectors that could cause tenant leakage or privacy issues. also look at how quantization might change tokenization or prefix stability.
[00:47] Sofia (Helios): yeah we've seen some odd cache-misses in production when we moved to an 8-bit qunatized model, and it changed some prompt outputs; not sure if it's tokenization or reranking.
[01:05] Priya (Redwood): okay, can you give a small example of the prompts that missed? you mentioned they are fairly templated?
[01:15] Sofia (Helios): um, yeah so a lot of requests are like \"context plus instruction\" patterns for motion planning. often identical prefixes besides a few dynamic sensor values. we saw the cache hit rate drop by maybe 12pct after quantization. our logs are a bit noisy tho.
[01:30] Marcus (Redwood): got it. so two threads: 1) cache key/schema — how we sign keys so identical logical prompts match even with noisy bits; and 2) tenant safety — ensure two tenants never accidentally share keys or responses.
[01:47] Tomas (Helios): also need to keep in mind our regulatory req: logs for inference must be retained in our VPC and redact PII.
[02:02] Jenna (Redwood): noted. i'll flag the private deploy checklist. let's jump into the proposed key scheme we sent earlier. Marcus, can you walk it?
[02:10] Marcus (Redwood): yeah, so the idea is a two-part signature: a normalized-prompt hash and a tenant-scoped salt. Normalization rules: strip non-deterministic timestamps, canonicalize white space, and optionally run application-level masking (e.g., replace sensor ids with stable tokens). then we compute H = HMAC-SHA256(tenant_salt, normalized_prompt_prefix). final key = tenant_id || \":" || base64(H[0:16]). this gives strong tenant isolation and small key sizes.
[02:45] Sofia (Helios): what's the chance of collision across tenants if tenant_id's are different?
[02:51] Marcus (Redwood): practically zero — HMAC with tenant salt means even same normalized prompt across tenants yields different H values. but the bigger risk is normalization mismatches: if Helios normalizes differently than runtime, you might get unintended misses.
[03:08] Ravi (Helios): can you handle different normalization rules per customer? we have some routes where we intentionally keep sensor offsets.
[03:16] Marcus (Redwood): yes, the runtime supports per-route normalization config; you can opt out of canonicalization for specific endpoint. drawback is lower hit rates.
[03:28] Lena (Helios): security question — who can read the raw prompt in logs? we need to prove that cached outputs are never materialized in plaintext outside our VPC.
[03:38] Priya (Redwood): for Redwood Private we offer log redaction and KMS-based encryption at rest. when deployed in your VPC, you can ensure logs never leave network boundaries and we can provide audit hooks. for hosted we do encryption but we can't meet that VPC isolation requirement.
[03:58] Tomas (Helios): ok that aligns. next on quantization: why would 8-bit qunatization drop hit rate?
[04:06] Marcus (Redwood): two effects: arithmetic noise may change generation probability mass slightly leading to different next-token choices when using sampling, but for prefix matching we only compare input prefixes. quantization can alter tokenization only if you use subword vocab or different pre/post-processing — usually tokenization is deterministic. the real issue is when the model's pre-processing pipeline normalizes or truncates differently after serialization. also if you run lower-precision encoder that approximates embeddings used in some cache-key approximations it can change fingerprinting.
[04:40] Sofia (Helios): we do use an embedding-based similarity fallback for soft hits. could quantization change embedding distances enough?
[04:48] Marcus (Redwood): yes, embedding drift is a thing especially with quantized models; we recommend a calibration step: run a smoke suite comparing fullprecision vs quantized embeddings on a heldout set and measure cosine drift; if > delta threshold you should prefer strict prefix-hash rather than embedding-based retrieval for critical routes.
[05:12] Ravi (Helios): can Redwood help run that calibration?
[05:16] Jenna (Redwood): yes — we'll include that as part of the bench. Marcus will run deterministic token and embedding comparison jobs.
[05:24] [06:00] (jump ahead) Marcus (Redwood): on hit-rate modeling, we took your anonymized 3-day trace sample and simulated a few policies: naive full-prompt keying, prefix-only (first N tokens), and normalized-prefix with masking. results: normalized-prefix at N=64 gave best tradeoff — hit-rate ~38% and no PII exposure on the sample, naive full-prompt 27% hit rate, prefix-only 44% but with higher exposure risk. caveat: sample had high template reuse.
[06:35] Sofia (Helios): how sensitive is that to N? our prompts vary a lot; sometimes only the first 20 tokens are stable.
[06:41] Marcus (Redwood): it depends. we provide a per-route optimizer that suggests N based on token-stability histogram. we also support adaptive prefix lengths so the system can use short prefix for low-latency routes and longer for batch-y routes.
[06:58] Lena (Helios): on the privacy side, if two tenants share the same model and a collision occurs — even if keys differ — could downstream caches leak an actual response? is there any cross-tenant memory that could be read?
[07:12] Priya (Redwood): by design each tenant's cache namespace is isolated at the key level in the runtime. for shared caches (e.g., memory-optimized shared L2), we still partition by tenant namespace and encrypt entries. we do have a safety check that prevents writing a cached response marked "sensitive" into shared cold-tier caches. That marking is decided by route config or on write-time heuristics.
[07:40] Tomas (Helios): what about race conditions with eviction where a later tenant reuses the same LRU slot? any chance of time-window leakage?
[07:48] Marcus (Redwood): time-window leakage is mitigated by namespace isolation; eviction reclaims slots but keys include tenant prefix so when slot reused the key won't match. the only scenario is if an attacker can tamper with the storage layer to bypass namespace checks — which on private deployments you control. but we'll provide attestation docs and an audit script.
[08:12] Ravi (Helios): ok good. let's talk about deterministic token experiments you mentioned.
[08:18] Marcus (Redwood): basic experiment: replay identical requests to full-precision and quantized runtime, record token-by-token deterministic equality, also capture embedding deltas for soft-match keys. we'll produce a per-route similarity report.
[08:33] Sofia (Helios): we can provide sample traces; will you accept masked tokens?
[08:37] Marcus (Redwood): yes, masked/anonymized traces are fine. we only need the structural pattern and token ids ideally. if not possible, timestamps and lengths are still useful.
[08:47] Jenna (Redwood): switching to operational constraints — Helios needs all audit logs in their VPC for six months. we support log forwarding via syslog/S3 connectors and you can set retention. do you need real-time streaming or batch?
[09:01] Lena (Helios): prefer streaming for incident response. also need RBAC where only security can view raw prompts. devs should only see metadata.
[09:12] Priya (Redwood): our Private control plane integrates with customer SSO and RBAC; we can restrict raw prompt access to roles and provide redact-at-ingest option.
[09:22] Tomas (Helios): for bench, do you need full traffic or sampled? sampling rate?
[09:27] Marcus (Redwood): sampled is fine — 1-5% should be enough for hit-rate estimation. include the templates and route mapping. we recommend sampling heavier on hot routes.
[09:36] Sofia (Helios): one more: how do you handle versioned models and cache invalidation on rollout?
[09:42] Marcus (Redwood): we tie cache namespace to model version hash by default; when you deploy new model variant we can either warm caches from the prior model or invalidate. warming is possible for compatible models — we use a migration path that re-hashes keys if normalization changes. automatic fallback is available so you can route <5% traffic to new model until warmed.
[10:00] Ravi (Helios): sounds good. any legal/regulatory concerns we should flag?
[10:05] Jenna (Redwood): main items: ensure prompt retention policies are documented in the contract addendum, confirm key custody for KMS, and include audit rights. we'll send a template.
[10:15] Lena (Helios): please send the SOC2 reports and the KMS integration docs.
[10:18] Jenna (Redwood): will do.
[10:22] [20:00] (skipping ahead) Marcus (Redwood): demo of an adaptive-prefix policy: we showed a quick console snippet where per-route you can set normalization, prefix length, and a \"sensitivity\" toggle. when sensitivity on, any candidate with PII marker is not allowed into shared cache and is routed to isolated reserved pool.
[20:30] Sofia (Helios): nice. does sensitivity detection run on-device?
[20:36] Marcus (Redwood): it can run either in your preprocessors or in the runtime. recommended is to run at-edge to minimize PII leaving the customer boundary. for hosted customers we provide a plugin but it's up to you.
[20:48] Tomas (Helios): how about cost/latency tradeoffs for isolated pools?
[20:53] Marcus (Redwood): isolated (dedicated) pools cost more but give consistent tail latency. for bursty workloads you can enable burst capacity. we provided a cost model in the deck — we'll reshare with Helios numbers for estimated tokens.
[21:10] Sofia (Helios): can we get an early pilot with a single route and 1 GPU reserved?
[21:15] Jenna (Redwood): yes, we typically run a pilot on a single route; we'll need SOW and pilot contract.
[21:22] [35:00] (later) Lena (Helios): quick security nit: what about side-channel leakage from quantized kernels? any CVE history?
[35:10] Priya (Redwood): we audit kernels and use AVX/AMX-safe implementations; known CVEs are patched in our runtime. for Private we can run a joint pentest. we'll include recent advisories.
[35:26] Ravi (Helios): ok, great.
[35:30] [50:00] Wrap-up: action items and next steps recapped. agreed pilot and bench.
[50:20] Jenna (Redwood): thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and schedule the bench run.
[50:30] Sofia (Helios): thanks, talk soon.

References shared: https://redwood.example.com/private-deploy-checklist (link), deck: \"Helios-prefix-proposal.pdf\" (uploaded to shared drive), benchmark sheet link: https://sheets.example.com/helios-bench (note: placeholder).

End of transcript.
